title: Buffers: bicarbonate and beta-alanine
goal: Explain how sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine buffer acid in blood and muscle, work out a bicarbonate dose, manage gut side effects and beta-alanine loading, and pick the events where they help.

steps.title: Two places to buffer acid
steps.text:
In *Lactate, H⁺ and fatigue* you saw that H⁺ does less harm inside the fibre than the old story said, yet in people making the blood more alkaline improves events of about **1–10 min** [[c:buf-alkalosis]]. Two supplements add [buffer](g:buffer), in two places:

| supplement | where it buffers | how fast |
|---|---|---|
| [sodium bicarbonate](g:sodium-bicarbonate) | blood, outside the muscle | one dose, hours before |
| [beta-alanine](g:beta-alanine) | inside the muscle, as [carnosine](g:carnosine) | daily for weeks |

Bicarbonate causes a mild [alkalosis](g:alkalosis) in the blood. The steeper [pH](g:ph) difference between muscle and blood then pulls more H⁺ and lactate out of the working muscle [[c:buf-gradient]].

claims.text: Induced acidosis worsens fatigue in whole-body exercise and alkalosis can improve performance in events of 1–10 minutes.

evidence.quote: In contrast, induced acidosis can exacerbate fatigue during whole-body dynamic exercise and alkalosis can improve exercise performance in events lasting 1-10 minutes.

claims.text: Bicarbonate acts as an extracellular buffer: raising blood pH and bicarbonate creates a gradient that draws H⁺ and lactate out of the exercising muscle; beta-alanine raises the muscle buffer carnosine.

evidence.quote: The resultant pH gradient between the intracellular and extracellular environments leads to efflux of H+ and La− from the exercising muscle.
A rate-limiting precursor to the endogenous intracellular (muscle) buffer, carnosine; the immediate defence against proton accumulation in the contracting musculature during exercise

steps.title: Bicarbonate: dose and timing
steps.text:
The ISSN position stand sets the dose by body mass [[c:buf-dose]]:

- **0.2 g·kg⁻¹** seems the minimum that works; **0.3 g·kg⁻¹** the best single dose.
- 0.4–0.5 g·kg⁻¹ adds no benefit, only more side effects.
- Take it **60–180 min** before the start.
- Or spread it: 0.4–0.5 g·kg⁻¹ a day in small doses for 3–7 days before the event.

The effect is modest: a [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) estimated about 1.7% more mean power in a single 1-min sprint at about 0.3 g·kg⁻¹, less in longer efforts [[c:buf-carr]]. The position stand's authors include several with supplement-industry ties.

claims.text: 0.2 g·kg⁻¹ sodium bicarbonate is the minimum and 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ the optimal single dose, taken 60–180 min before; 0.4–0.5 g·kg⁻¹ adds side effects, not benefit; multi-day protocols use 0.4–0.5 g·kg⁻¹ per day for 3–7 days.

evidence.quote: For single-dose supplementation protocols, 0.2 g/kg of sodium bicarbonate seems to be the minimum dose required to experience improvements in exercise performance. The optimal dose of sodium bicarbonate dose for ergogenic effects seems to be 0.3 g/kg.
For single-dose supplementation protocols, the recommended timing of sodium bicarbonate ingestion is between 60 and 180 min before exercise or competition.

Higher doses (e.g., 0.4 or 0.5 g/kg) may not be required in single-dose supplementation protocols, because they do not provide additional benefits (compared with 0.3 g/kg) and are associated with a higher incidence and severity of adverse side-effects.
The duration of these protocols is generally between 3 and 7 days before the exercise test, and a total sodium bicarbonate dose of 0.4 or 0.5 g/kg per day produces ergogenic effects.
Single acute NaHCO 3 dose of 0.2–0.4 g/kg BM, consumed 60–150 min prior to exercise

claims.text: Sodium bicarbonate at about 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ raised mean power by about 1.7% in a single 1-min sprint, with smaller effects in longer tests.

evidence.quote: The remaining 38 studies and 137 estimates for sodium bicarbonate produced a possibly moderate performance enhancement of 1.7% (90% CL ± 2.0%) with a typical dose of 3.5 mmoL/kg/BM (∼0.3 g/kg/BM) in a single 1-minute sprint, following blinded consumption by male athletes.
a reduction of 0.6% (±0.9%) for each 10-fold increase in test duration (e.g. 1-10 minutes)

steps.title: Working out a bicarbonate dose
steps.problem: A 64 kg runner wants the optimal single dose of sodium bicarbonate before a 1500 m race. How many grams?
steps: Timing: 60–180 min before; the long end of that window (about 180 min), with a meal, is kinder to the gut.
Compare caffeine at 3–6 mg·kg⁻¹: 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ is 300 mg·kg⁻¹, 50–100 times more, so bicarbonate is counted in grams.

steps.title: The catch: the gut
steps.text:
Bicarbonate's main problem is the gut. The common side effects are bloating, nausea, vomiting and stomach pain; they vary between and within people, and can wreck the performance they were meant to help [[c:buf-gi]].

Ways to lower the risk:

- a smaller dose (0.2 or 0.3 g·kg⁻¹, not more)
- take it about 180 min before, or find your own best time
- with a carbohydrate-rich meal
- in enteric-coated capsules (they dissolve past the stomach)
- a multi-day protocol, so race day needs no big dose

One more twist: part of bicarbonate's effect seems to come from [placebo](g:placebo) [[c:buf-placebo]].

claims.text: The commonest side effects of sodium bicarbonate are bloating, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain; smaller doses, ~180 min timing, a high-carbohydrate meal and enteric-coated capsules can reduce them.

evidence.quote: The most common side-effects of sodium bicarbonate supplementation are bloating, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The incidence and severity of side-effects vary between and within individuals, but it is generally low. Nonetheless, these side-effects following sodium bicarbonate supplementation may negatively impact exercise performance.

Ingesting sodium bicarbonate (i) in smaller doses (e.g., 0.2 g/kg or 0.3 g/kg), (ii) around 180 min before exercise or adjusting the timing according to individual responses to side-effects, (iii) alongside a high-carbohydrate meal, and (iv) in enteric-coated capsules are possible strategies to minimize the likelihood and severity of these side-effects.

claims.text: Part of sodium bicarbonate's ergogenic effect seems to be placebo-driven.

evidence.quote: Still, a portion of the ergogenic effect of sodium bicarbonate seems to be placebo-driven.

steps.title: Beta-alanine: building the muscle's own buffer
steps.text:
Beta-alanine works differently. The muscle needs it to make carnosine, so a supplement raises carnosine slowly, day by day [[c:buf-ba-carnosine]]:

| daily 4–6 g, split | muscle carnosine |
|---|---|
| 2 weeks | +20–30% |
| 4 weeks | +40–60% |
| 10 weeks | up to +80% |

One dose on race morning does nothing for carnosine. Large single doses cause [paraesthesia](g:paraesthesia): harmless pins and needles in the skin. Smaller split doses (about 1.6 g) or slow-release tablets reduce it [[c:buf-ba-tingle]]. Responses vary: some people raise carnosine much less than others [[c:buf-ba-vary]].

claims.text: 4–6 g of beta-alanine daily raises muscle carnosine by 20–30% after 2 weeks, 40–60% after 4 weeks and up to 80% after 10 weeks.

evidence.quote: Four weeks of beta-alanine supplementation (4-6 g daily) significantly augments muscle carnosine concentrations, thereby acting as an intracellular pH buffer
for a minimum of two weeks (which results in a 20-30 % increase in muscle carnosine concentrations) [ 4 ], with greater benefits seen after 4 weeks (40-60 % increase)
and up to 80 % after 10 weeks

claims.text: The only reported side effect of beta-alanine is paraesthesia, reduced by divided lower doses (1.6 g) or a sustained-release form.

evidence.quote: The only reported side effect is paraesthesia (tingling), but studies indicate this can be attenuated by using divided lower doses (1.6 g) or using a sustained-release formula

claims.text: After 5–6 weeks of 4.8 g·day⁻¹ beta-alanine, high responders raised muscle carnosine by about 55% and low responders by about 15%.

evidence.quote: individuals vary in the magnitude of response to 5 to 6 weeks of beta-alanine supplementation (4.8 g/day), with high responders increasing muscle carnosine concentrations by an average of 55 %, and low responders increasing by an average of only 15 %

steps.title: Which events?
steps.text:
Both buffers help the same window: hard efforts of about **30 s to 10 min**. For bicarbonate, the effect is clearest around 1 min and fades beyond 10 min [[c:buf-ioc-window]].

For beta-alanine, a meta-analysis of 40 studies (1,461 people) found a small overall effect (0.18). Within 0.5–10 min, it was clear in [time-to-exhaustion](g:time-to-exhaustion) tests (0.50) but not in time trials (0.11, [confidence interval](g:confidence-interval) crossing zero) [[c:buf-saunders]]. Races are time trials, and time-to-exhaustion tests tend to show bigger changes.

So: a 4 km track pursuit, a 1500 m or a 400 m swim, yes maybe; a marathon or a 70.3, no.

claims.text: Bicarbonate enhances ~60 s sprints by about 2%, with reduced efficacy beyond 10 min; beta-alanine gives small benefits in tasks of 30 s to 10 min, harder to realise in well-trained athletes.

evidence.quote: Enhanced performance (~2%) of short-term, high-intensity sprints lasting ~60 s in duration, with a reduced efficacy as the effort duration exceeds 10 min
Small, but potentially meaningful performance benefits (~0.2%–3%) during both continuous and intermittent exercise tasks of 30 s to 10 min in duration

claims.text: Across 40 studies (1,461 participants), beta-alanine had a small overall effect (0.18); within 0.5–10 min, effects were larger for exercise capacity (0.50) than performance (0.11, CI crossing zero).

evidence.quote: 40 individual studies employing 65 different exercise protocols and totalling 70 exercise measures in 1461 participants were included in the analyses. A significant overall effect size of 0.18 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.28) was shown.

Subgroup analyses also identified the type of exercise as a significant (p=0.013) moderator of effect sizes within an exercise time frame of 0.5-10 min with greater effect sizes for exercise capacity (0.4998 (95% CI 0.246 to 0.753)) versus performance (0.1078 (95% CI -0.201 to 0.416)).

points: Bicarbonate buffers in the blood and draws H⁺ out of muscle; beta-alanine builds carnosine, a buffer inside the muscle.
Bicarbonate: 0.2 g·kg⁻¹ minimum, 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ best, 60–180 min before (dose = body mass × g per kg). Gains about 1.7% in a 1-min sprint.
Gut trouble is the catch: smaller dose, about 180 min before, with a carbohydrate meal, or enteric-coated capsules.
Beta-alanine: 4–6 g a day in split doses for at least 2–4 weeks; one race-day dose only tingles.
Both help hard efforts of about 30 s to 10 min, not marathons or long triathlons. In time trials, beta-alanine's effect is small and uncertain.

variants.stem: Where does each supplement add buffering?

options.text: Bicarbonate in the blood; beta-alanine inside the muscle
options.why: Right: bicarbonate is an extracellular buffer; beta-alanine raises carnosine in the fibres.

options.text: Bicarbonate inside the muscle; beta-alanine in the blood
options.why: Reversed: carnosine is a muscle buffer, bicarbonate works from the blood.
Bicarbonate stays mostly outside the fibre and draws H⁺ out.
Carnosine sits inside the muscle fibres.

variants.stem: An 80 kg cyclist wants the optimal single dose of sodium bicarbonate before a 4 km pursuit. How much?

options.why: Right: 80 kg × 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ = 24 g.
Grams per kg read as mg per kg: 1,000 times too small.
This uses 0.5 g·kg⁻¹, which adds side effects, not benefit.
This is the minimum, 0.2 g·kg⁻¹, not the optimal 0.3.

variants.stem: A 55 kg swimmer has gut trouble and wants the lowest dose that works. How much sodium bicarbonate?

options.why: Right: 55 kg × 0.2 g·kg⁻¹ = 11 g.
This is 0.3 g·kg⁻¹, the optimal dose, not the minimum.
Grams per kg read as mg per kg: 1,000 times too small.
This uses 0.5 g·kg⁻¹, the worst choice for her gut.

variants.stem: In the meta-analysis, about how much did 0.3 g·kg⁻¹ bicarbonate raise mean power in a single 1-min sprint?

options.why: Right: a modest gain, with a wide uncertainty (±2.0%).
Ten times too big: buffer gains are small.
Too small: 1.7% was estimated, though with wide uncertainty.
Too big: the estimate was 1.7%, give or take 2.0%.

variants.stem: A 1500 m runner took 0.4 g·kg⁻¹ bicarbonate 45 min before a race and vomited. Best change?

options.text: 0.2–0.3 g·kg⁻¹, about 180 min before, with a carb-rich meal
options.why: Right: smaller dose, longer gap, food: the main ways to reduce gut trouble.

options.text: Same dose, but 15 min before so it can't upset her
options.why: Less time doesn't help; the advice is longer, around 180 min.

options.text: Same dose on an empty stomach
options.why: A carbohydrate-rich meal reduces side effects.

options.text: A bigger dose so less is needed later
options.why: Bigger doses raise side effects without extra benefit.

variants.stem: A triathlete takes 3 g beta-alanine for the first time 30 min before a sprint-distance race. Will it help?

options.text: No: carnosine takes weeks of daily doses to rise
options.why: Right: 2–4 weeks of 4–6 g a day are needed; one dose mostly gives tingling.

options.text: Yes: it buffers acid in the blood within 30 min
options.why: That's bicarbonate's route; beta-alanine works by building carnosine.
Caffeine doesn't speed up carnosine loading.

options.text: No: beta-alanine only works in men
options.why: Nothing suggests a sex difference; the problem is timing.

variants.stem: A track cyclist loading beta-alanine gets strong tingling after each 3.2 g dose. Best fix?

options.text: Split it into 1.6 g doses, or use slow-release
options.why: Right: smaller divided doses or a sustained-release form reduce paraesthesia.
The tingling is harmless and passes.

options.text: Take the whole daily dose at once to get it over with
options.why: Large single doses cause the tingling.

options.text: Switch to taking it only on race day
options.why: Then carnosine never rises: it needs weeks of daily intake.

variants.stem: Which athlete is most likely to gain from sodium bicarbonate?

options.text: A cyclist riding a 4 km pursuit (about 4–5 min)
options.why: Right: buffers help hard efforts of about 30 s to 10 min.
The effect fades beyond 10 min, and the gut risk is high for a long race.
Far beyond the 1–10 min window where buffering helps.

options.text: A cyclist riding a 100 km sportive
options.why: Long steady efforts aren't limited by acid build-up in the same way.

variants.stem: Beta-alanine's effect was 0.50 in time-to-exhaustion tests but 0.11 (CI crossing zero) in time trials. Which matters for a racer, and why?

options.text: The time-trial effect: races are like time trials
options.why: Right: time-to-exhaustion tests tend to magnify changes; the race-like result is small and uncertain.

options.text: The 0.50: it's the bigger, clearer number
options.why: Bigger isn't more relevant; the test should look like the race.

options.text: Neither: effect sizes can't be compared
options.why: Both are standardised effect sizes; comparing them is the point.
Averaging two different tests hides the one that matches the race.
